description: Cosmic Kin is a parent–daughter team combining two generations of curiosity, creativity and technology. For NASA Space Apps 2026, we're building EarthEcho, an interactive listening observatory that transforms real Earth science observations into sound. Our interests include space science, accessible technology, creative coding, data visualization and educational experiences. We believe exploring our planet should be exciting and accessible to everyone.
summary:
What if we could hear Earth's changing story?

EarthEcho is an interactive listening observatory that transforms real Arctic sea-ice measurements into music, making environmental science engaging and accessible through sound.

Using NASA Earth imagery and satellite-derived sea-ice observations published by NSIDC, EarthEcho creates reproducible musical signatures for every month of 2024. Greater ice extent produces higher notes, while seasonal changes influence melody and rhythm.

Visitors explore an interactive 3D Earth, listen to the Ice Symphony, compare scientific observations, and participate in Sonic Lens, an interactive challenge where they identify environmental differences through sound before revealing the actual measurements.

Developed by Cosmic Kin, a parent–daughter team, EarthEcho combines scientific accuracy, creative technology, and inclusive educational design to demonstrate how Earth's environmental information can be understood through more than one sense.
details:
EarthEcho — The Listening Observatory

The Challenge

Earth science is often communicated through maps, satellite imagery and numerical charts. While these are scientifically valuable, they can be difficult to interpret without relying on sight.

For NASA Space Apps 2026's The Earth Information Jukebox challenge, our parent–daughter team, Cosmic Kin, developed EarthEcho to explore how environmental observations can become meaningful listening experiences.

Our Solution

EarthEcho is a browser-based scientific observatory that translates twelve monthly Arctic sea-ice extent measurements from 2024 into original, data-driven sound.

It combines a realistic interactive 3D Earth, scientific charts, musical experiences and listening-based discovery activities.

Key Features

Interactive 3D Earth: Visitors rotate, zoom and explore Earth, focus on the Arctic and see an equal-area reference ring corresponding to the selected measurement. The ring illustrates measured area, not the actual geographic shape of sea ice.

Listen to Earth: Each month produces a deterministic musical signature. Ice extent influences pitch, while the direction and magnitude of change influence melody and rhythm.

The Ice Symphony: A guided three-chapter experience communicates the seasonal maximum, summer retreat and return of Arctic sea ice using music, measurements and explanatory captions.

Sonic Lens: Visitors listen to two hidden observations, predict which represents greater sea-ice extent and then reveal the scientific evidence. Four rounds encourage learning through listening.

Compare Moments: Visitors compare two months through measurements, differences and original sound signatures.

Sound DNA: Scientific measurements, musical notes, frequencies and sound-mapping rules are explained transparently.

Science View: A polar scientific map and an optional NASA visualization-frame analyzer allow visitors to explore how visual characteristics can also influence sound.

Scientific Methodology

Our numerical observations come from the National Snow and Ice Data Center's Sea Ice Index, Version 3.

The sound engine uses reproducible mathematical mappings. Larger sea-ice extent corresponds to a higher musical register. Growing and retreating measurements influence melodic direction, while the magnitude of change influences rhythmic activity.

NASA's Blue Marble and Earth-at-night composites provide the globe's geographic appearance. NASA Scientific Visualization Studio's Arctic sea-ice products provide additional scientific visualization context.

The application distinguishes actual measurements, scientific visualizations and artistic interpretations. Seasonal changes during 2024 are not presented as proof of a long-term climate trend.

Technology

EarthEcho uses HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, three.js, WebGL, Web Audio API, Canvas and SVG.

The application is packaged as a self-contained browser experience. Its musical sounds are synthesized procedurally, without third-party music recordings.

Creativity and Impact

EarthEcho's main innovation is its Listen → Interpret → Reveal → Understand interaction.

Rather than simply displaying environmental data, EarthEcho gives people another way to investigate it. Users can hear differences, form hypotheses, and connect musical patterns to scientific evidence.

The project is intended for students, educators, science museums and anyone interested in exploring environmental information through multiple senses.

Accessibility-oriented features include keyboard controls, readable measurement data, explanations, captions, audio controls and reduced-motion support.

Further testing with blind and low-vision participants would be valuable before making broader accessibility claims.

Future Potential

The same scientific sonification approach could be extended to other NASA Earth Information Center datasets, creating new listening experiences for precipitation, ocean temperatures and other environmental observations.

EarthEcho demonstrates how scientific accuracy, accessible design and creative technology can make Earth science more engaging for future generations.
